docs.plain:
Ocean Tides

What you will learn
- Explain what causes the two daily tidal bulges.
- Describe the difference between spring tides and neap tides.
- Calculate the tidal range from high and low water heights.

Why the ocean rises and falls
- Water in the ocean is pulled by gravity, and the pull is stronger on the side of Earth that faces the Moon.
- KEY POINT: Tides are caused mainly by the gravitational pull of the Moon, with a smaller contribution from the Sun.
- A tidal bulge on the far side of Earth forms because Earth is pulled away from the water there.
- Because Earth turns beneath these two bulges, the water level at a coast rises and falls twice a day.
- KEY POINT: Most coasts have two high tides and two low tides every lunar day of about 24 hours and 50 minutes.
- Sailors use tide tables to plan when to enter shallow harbours. Salt marshes depend on the regular flooding and draining caused by the tides. The Mediterranean Sea has very small tides because it is almost enclosed.
Speaker notes: Expect an exam question on this.

Words for the water level
- Flood tide is the rising water and ebb tide is the falling water.
- Slack water is the short time at high or low tide when the water is neither rising nor falling.

Spring tides and neap tides
- KEY POINT: Spring tides happen at new moon and full moon, when the Sun, Earth and Moon line up.
- KEY POINT: Neap tides happen at the first and third quarter moons, when the Sun and Moon pull at right angles.
Speaker notes: This is the part that examiners always test.

Measuring tidal range
- The tidal range is the difference in height between high water and the next low water.
- For example, with a high water of 4.5 m and a low water of 1.2 m, the range is 4.5 m minus 1.2 m, which is 3.3 m.
- Tidal range is largest in narrow funnel-shaped bays such as the Bay of Fundy , where it can pass fifteen metres.

Practice
- Exercise 1: The high water height is 4.5 m and the low water height is 1.2 m. What is the tidal range?
- Exercise 2: Why is the tidal range so large in the Bay of Fundy?
- Exercise 3: What do we call the short time at high or low tide when the water neither rises nor falls?

Summary
- Tides are caused mainly by the Moon's pull, with a smaller contribution from the Sun.
- Spring tides come at new moon and full moon, when the Sun, Earth and Moon line up.
- Neap tides come at the first and third quarter moons, when the Sun and Moon pull at right angles.
- Most coasts have two high tides and two low tides every lunar day.

How Vaccines Train the Immune System

Learning goals

• Describe how a vaccine prepares the body for a real infection.

• Explain why some vaccines need booster doses.

Antigens and antibodies

An antigen is a molecule that the immune system recognises as foreign. Antibodies are proteins that attach to one specific antigen and mark it for destruction.

Key idea: A vaccine shows the immune system a harmless version of an antigen so that it can respond faster to the real one.

Don't forget that the first meeting with an antigen is slow, while later meetings are much faster.

Memory cells stay in the body for years and let the immune system answer a repeated infection within days.

Kinds of vaccine

Live attenuated vaccines contain a weakened form of the germ. Inactivated vaccines contain a germ that has been killed. Messenger RNA vaccines carry instructions that let our own cells build a harmless piece of the germ.

Inactivated vaccines usually need booster doses because they produce a weaker memory response.

Make sure you can explain why boosters are needed. This will be tested.

Herd protection

When most people in a community are immune, the germ struggles to find new hosts, and even unvaccinated people are less likely to meet it.

Important: Herd protection depends on a high share of the community being immune, not on any single person.

Babies too young to be vaccinated are protected mainly by the immunity of the people around them.

Check your understanding

Question 1: Why does a second dose of an inactivated vaccine strengthen the response?

Question 2: What is the job of an antibody?

Question 3: Why are babies too young to be vaccinated still protected in a community with high immunity?

To sum up

• A vaccine shows the immune system a harmless version of an antigen so that it can respond faster to the real one.

• Inactivated vaccines usually need booster doses.

• Herd protection depends on a high share of the community being immune.

How a Bill Becomes Law in a Two-Chamber Legislatu
Why the process matters
A legislature makes laws by following a set of rules for introducing, debating, revising, and approving bills. In a two-chamber legislature, the process is designed to give ideas careful consideration and to prevent one chamber from acting alone. The chambers may disagree about a proposal, but both must generally approve the same final text before it can become law.
KEY POINT: The central rule: A bill usually needs approval from both chambers, and the president or other executive official must also sign the bill or allow it to become law without a signature.
1. The bill is drafted
A law begins as an idea. A member, committee, government agency, or interested organization may propose a policy. Drafters then turn that idea into bill language, often called the bill's text. A sponsor formally introduces the bill and becomes the legislator most responsible for guiding it through the legislature.
The process varies somewhat among states and countries, but many legislatures use a similar committee system. Legislative staff may research the issue, check legal language, and prepare amendments. The sponsor may also consult colleagues or hold public meetings to build support.
2. Introduction and first reading
A bill is introduced into one chamber by its sponsor or by a committee. The bill is assigned a number, printed, and placed on the chamber's calendar. The title is read, and the measure may be referred to the appropriate committee.
A first reading introduces the proposal for formal consideration. Some chambers use first reading mainly for identification and procedural notice, while others require committees to hold separate public hearings. At this stage, the bill is often not yet approved in substance.
3. Committee review
Committees are where much of the detailed work happens. Members receive the bill, hold hearings, invite witnesses, and discuss possible changes. Interested members of the public, agencies, businesses, and advocacy groups may submit testimony.
After reviewing the proposal, a committee may:
- approve the bill unchanged;
- approve it with amendments;

- substitute a different bill;
- merge it with another measure;
- hold it for further study; or
- report that it should not advance.
KEY POINT: Remember: A hearing collects information, but passage still requires votes from the full membership of the chamber.
4. Floor debate and voting
If a committee recommends advancing the bill, it returns to the chamber floor. Legislators debate the proposal and may offer amendments. The rules of each chamber determine how much debate is allowed, how amendments are considered, and when the vote occurs.
The chamber then votes on the bill. A simple majority is often enough for ordinary legislation, although some measures require a larger majority. If the bill passes, it moves to the second chamber with the text approved by the first chamber.
5. Action in the second chamber
The second chamber receives the bill and repeats many of the same steps. A committee may hold new hearings because that chamber's members may have different questions or priorities. The bill can be approved, amended, merged with related legislation, or defeated.
This stage is essential because reviewing the proposal in a separate chamber can reveal costs, unintended effects, conflicts with existing laws, or opportunities for improvement.
If the second chamber approves a different version of the bill, the proposal does not automatically become law. Usually, a conference committee made up of members from both chambers meets to negotiate a single final text.
6. Conference committee
A conference committee is not a third chamber. It is a temporary group of legislators from both chambers. Its task is to resolve disagreements and recommend one version of the bill.
Both chambers must then approve the conference report. The chambers often vote on the negotiated proposal again rather than reopening every earlier amendment one by one.
7. Final approval
After both chambers agree on the same text, the bill is sent to the executive, such as a governor, president, or monarch. The executive may sign it, veto it, take no action, or in some systems use a veto override.
If the executive vetoes the bill, the legislature may reconsider it. A veto override commonly requires a supermajority, such as two-thirds or three-fourths of the members voting.

A bill becomes law only after completing every required stage. That means approval by both chambers and completion of the executive review process.
KEY POINT: The final checkpoint: Do not stop after the second chamber's vote. The bill must also clear executive review.
Common points of confusion
- The bill's introduction is not its passage.
- Committee approval is not final passage by the legislature.
- Approval of different amendments in two chambers does not settle the matter.
- A conference report is only a recommendation until both chambers accept it.
- A veto does not always end the legislative process.
- The version enacted is the final version approved through the required process.
Summary
A bill begins with an idea and formal drafting, enters one chamber through introduction, and is studied by a committee. After debate and a floor vote, it moves to the second chamber. If the chambers approve different texts, a conference committee helps reconcile them. Both chambers must approve the same final version, which is then sent to the executive. Only after all required approvals and any applicable veto proceedings are completed does the bill become law.
Exercises
1. In your own words, explain why a bill needs to pass through two separate chambers.
2. What is the difference between committee approval and passage by the full chamber?
3. What happens if the two chambers approve different versions of the same bill?
4. Why is a conference committee described as temporary rather than as a third chamber?
5. Why must an executive consider a bill after both chambers have acted?
6. Put the stages in order: executive review, committee hearing, introduction, conference
committee, second-chamber vote.
7. A chamber approves a bill by a simple majority. Is that enough to make it law? Explain.
8. Name two actions an executive might take after receiving a bill.
9. Why might a chamber hold a new hearing after the other chamber has already studied a
bill?
10. How does a veto override differ from ordinary passage?

docs.plain:
The Basics of Compound Interest and the Rule of 72

Compound interest is often called the *eighth wonder of the world* because of its power to grow wealth exponentially over time. Unlike simple interest, which is calculated only on the original principal, compound interest earns interest on both the initial amount and the accumulated interest from previous periods. This means your money grows faster the longer it is invested.

How Compound Interest Works

The formula for compound interest is:

A = P(1 + r/n)^(nt)

- A = the amount of money accumulated after n years, including interest.

- P = the principal amount (the initial amount of money).

- r = the annual interest rate (decimal).

- n = the number of times interest is compounded per year.

- t = the time the money is invested for, in years.

For example, if you invest $1,000 at an annual interest rate of 5% compounded annually for 10 years, the calculation would be:

A = 1000(1 + 0.05/1)^(1*10) = $1,628.89

Notice how the investment grows not just by a fixed amount each year, but by an increasing amount as interest is added to the principal.

The Power of Time

One of the most important factors in compound interest is time. The longer your money is invested, the more dramatic the growth. This is why starting to invest early is so critical. Even small amounts can grow into substantial sums over decades.

Remember: Time in the market often beats timing the market.

The Rule of 72

The Rule of 72 is a simple way to estimate how long it will take for an investment to double at a given annual rate of return. To use it, divide 72 by the annual interest rate (as a percentage). The result is the approximate number of years it will take for the investment to double.

For example:

- At a 6% annual return, an investment will double in 72 / 6 = 12 years.

- At a 9% annual return, it will double in 72 / 9 = 8 years.

This rule is particularly useful for quick mental calculations and financial planning. While it’s an approximation, it’s remarkably accurate for interest rates between 6% and 10%.

Why It Matters

Understanding compound interest and the Rule of 72 helps you make smarter financial decisions. Whether you're saving for retirement, a house, or your child's education, these concepts show you the importance of starting early and staying consistent.

Exercises

1. If you invest $5,000 at an annual interest rate of 7% compounded annually, how much will you have after 15 years?

2. Using the Rule of 72, how long will it take for an investment to double at an 8% annual return?

3. Compare the future value of $1,000 invested at 5% simple interest vs. 5% compound interest for 10 years.

Summary

- Compound interest grows your money exponentially by earning interest on interest.

- The Rule of 72 is a quick way to estimate doubling time for investments.

- Time is your greatest ally in compounding—start early to maximize growth.

Similarly, it gives in Chapter III only those principles of the paragraph and the sentence which are of the widest application. The book thus covers only a small portion of the field of English style. The experience of its writer has been that once past the essentials, students profit most by individual instruction based on the problems of their own work, and that each instructor has his own body of theory, which he may prefer to that offered by any textbook. The numbers of the sections may be used as references in correcting manuscript. Kelley, _Workmanship in Words_ (Little, Brown and Co.). In these will be found full discussions of many points here briefly treated and an abundant store of illustrations to supplement those given in this book. It is an old observation that the best writers sometimes disregard the rules of rhetoric. When they do so, however, the reader will usually find in the sentence some compensating merit, attained at the cost of the violation. Unless he is certain of doing as well, he will probably do best to follow the rules. After he has learned, by their guidance, to write plain English adequate for everyday uses, let him look, for the secrets of style, to the study of the masters of literature. II. ELEMENTARY RULES OF USAGE 1. Form the possessive singular of nouns by adding 's. Follow this rule whatever the final consonant. Thus write, Charles's friend Burns's poems the witch's malice This is the usage of the United States Government Printing Office and of the Oxford University Press. Exceptions are the possessive of ancient proper names in _-es_ and _-is_, the possessive _Jesus'_, and such forms as _for conscience' sake_, _for righteousness' sake_. But such forms as _Achilles' heel_, _Moses' laws_, _Isis' temple_ are commonly replaced by the heel of Achilles the laws

of Moses the temple of Isis The pronominal possessives _hers_, _its_, _theirs_, _yours_, and _oneself_ have no apostrophe. 2. In a series of three or more terms with a single conjunction, use a comma after each term except the last. Thus write, red, white, and blue gold, silver, or copper He opened the letter, read it, and made a note of its contents. This is also the usage of the Government Printing Office and of the Oxford University Press. In the names of business firms the last comma is omitted, as, Brown, Shipley & Co. 3. Enclose parenthetic expressions between commas. The best way to see a country, unless you are pressed for time, is to travel on foot. This rule is difficult to apply; it is frequently hard to decide whether a single word, such as _however_, or a brief phrase, is or is not parenthetic. If the interruption to the flow of the sentence is but slight, the writer may safely omit the commas. But whether the interruption be slight or considerable, he must never insert one comma and omit the other. Such punctuation as Marjorie's husband, Colonel Nelson paid us a visit yesterday, or My brother you will be pleased to hear, is now in perfect health, is indefensible. If a parenthetic expression is preceded by a conjunction, place the first comma before the conjunction, not after it. He saw us coming, and unaware that we had learned of his treachery, greeted us with a smile. The audience, which had at first been indifferent, became more and more interested. The sentence is virtually a combination of two statements which might have been made independently: The audience had at first been indifferent. It became more and more interested. Here the clause introduced by _who_ does serve to tell which of several possible candidates is meant; the sentence cannot be split up into two independent statements. The day will come when you will admit your mistake. Nether Stowey is completely identified by its name; the statement about Coleridge is therefore supplementary and parenthetic. The _day_ spoken of is identified only by the dependent clause, which is therefore restrictive. Similar in principle to the enclosing of parenthetic expressions between commas is the setting off by commas of phrases or dependent clauses preceding or following the main clause of a sentence. Partly by hard fighting, partly by diplomatic skill, they enlarged their dominions to the east, and rose to royal rank with the possession of Sicily, exchanged afterwards for Sardinia. Other illustrations may be found in sentences quoted under Rules 4, 5, 6, 7, 16, and 18. The writer should be careful not to set off independent clauses by commas: see under Rule 5. 4. The water of the downpour would have rushed by us, muddy with the spoils of the rocks, coming together into torrents, cutting deep gorges and canyons as they hurried past to deposit their sediment in the earliest seas. Through the clouds we should have glimpsed a great sun moving visibly across the sky, and in its wake and in the wake of the moon would have come a diurnal tide of earthquake and upheaval. And

the moon, which nowadays keeps one constant face to earth, would then have been rotating visibly and showing the side it now hides so inexorably.

The earth aged. One million years followed another, and the day lengthened, the sun grew more distant and milder, the moon’s pace in the sky slackened; the intensity of rain and storm diminished and the water in the first seas increased and ran together into the ocean garment our planet henceforth wore.

But there was no life as yet upon the earth; the seas were lifeless, and the rocks were barren.

III THE BEGINNINGS OF LIFE

As everybody knows nowadays, the knowledge we possess of life before the beginnings of human memory and tradition is derived from the markings and fossils of living things in the stratified rocks. We find preserved in shale and slate, limestone, and sandstone, bones, shells, fibres, stems, fruits, footmarks, scratchings and the like, side by side with the ripple marks of the earliest tides and the pittings of the earliest rain-falls. It is by the sedulous examination of this Record of the Rocks that the past history of the earth’s life has been pieced together. That much nearly everybody knows to-day. The sedimentary rocks do not lie neatly stratum above stratum; they have been crumpled, bent, thrust about, distorted and mixed together like the leaves of a library that has been repeatedly looted and burnt, and it is only as a result of many devoted lifetimes of work that the record has been put into order and read. The whole compass of time represented by the record of the rocks is now estimated as 1,600,000,000 years.

The earliest rocks in the record are called by geologists the Azoic rocks, because they show no traces of life. Great areas of these Azoic rocks lie uncovered in North America, and they are of such a thickness that geologists consider that they represent a period of at least half of the 1,600,000,000 which they assign to the whole geological record. Let me repeat this profoundly significant fact. Half the great interval of time since land and sea were first distinguishable on earth has left us no traces of life. There are ripplings and rain marks still to be found in these rocks, but no marks nor vestiges of any living thing.

MARINE LIFE IN THE CAMBRIAN PERIOD MARINE LIFE IN THE CAMBRIAN PERIOD 1 and 8, Jellyfishes; 2, Hyolithes (swimming snail); 3, Humenocaris; 4, Protospongia; 5, Lampshells (Obolella); 6, Orthoceras; 7, Trilobite (Paradoxides) — see fossil on page 13; 9, Coral (Archæocyathus); 10, Bryograptus; 11, Trilobite (Olenellus); 12, Palesterina

Then, as we come up the record, signs of past life appear and increase. The age of the world’s history in which we find these past traces is called by geologists the Lower Palæozoic age. The first indications that life was astir are vestiges of comparatively simple and lowly things: the shells of small shellfish, the stems and flowerlike heads of zoophytes, seaweeds and the tracks and remains of sea worms and crustacea. [0:00] Welcome back. Today we are talking about ocean tides, and I want to get the big ideas straight. Tides are caused mainly by the gravitational pull of the Moon, with a smaller contribution from the Sun. I will say that again, because it is the single most important idea today.
[0:46] Tides are caused mainly by the gravitational pull of the Moon, with a smaller contribution from the Sun. This will be on the exam, so write it down. Most coasts have two high tides and two low tides every lunar day of about twenty four hours and fifty minutes.
[1:32] Remember that, because it explains why the times shift every day. Next, spring tides happen at new moon and full moon, when the Sun, Earth and Moon line up. Pay attention to this one, it comes up in every problem set.
[2:14] Neap tides happen at the first and third quarter moons, when the Sun and Moon pull at right angles. Make sure you can tell spring tides from neap tides. Now a definition. The tidal range is the difference in height between high water and the next low water.
[3:00] Note that tidal range is largest in narrow funnel shaped bays such as the Bay of Fundy. Sailors use tide tables to plan when to enter shallow harbours. Salt marshes depend on the regular flooding and draining caused by the tides.
[3:43] The Mediterranean Sea has very small tides because it is almost enclosed. That is all for today. Think about spring tides and neap tides before next time.
